title: An early feasibility study evaluating a novel device for identifying seizure activity in a sample of 15 children
official: Accessible continuous electroencephalography and swift screening for epilepsy diagnosis and management in children and young people
summary:
Background and study aims
Epilepsy affects over half a million people in the UK, with children and the elderly having the highest occurrences. Children with epilepsy can experience lifelong health, developmental and psychological challenges. Confirming a diagnosis of suspected epilepsy is often costly in terms of time, as waiting lists of 6-8 weeks for an outpatient-based routine 30-minute electroencephalography (EEG) can delay a diagnosis and may not provide the necessary information required due to the nature of the seizures and the timing of the EEG monitoring. The lengthy diagnostic process is costly to the UK in terms of hospital-based care required and days lost through poor control of seizures. Misdiagnosis of epilepsy further delays the correct treatment and can lead to hospital admissions, side effects and reduced quality of life. For patients experiencing long-term complicated seizures despite medication, in-hospital video EEG monitoring maintained over 3-5 days offers more accurate clinical information and the chance of a confirmed diagnosis. Capacity for this type of monitoring throughout the UK is severely limited, with waiting times of several months to over a year. The device we are investigating, Clic EEG, has the ability to record EEG data and is wireless, which permits the wearer to be independent. Data from the device/devices can be downloaded via a docking station or transmitted wirelessly to a computer. The devices can be worn for up to 48 hours and then changed for new devices offering up to 5 days of EEG monitoring.
The aim of the study is to generate clinical evidence on the ability of Clic EEG to provide sufficient seizure data comparable with the gold standard video EEG monitoring as provided in hospital-based care. The study aims to recruit 15 participants to receive the intervention and five further health care professionals to complete questionnaires and interviews on the acceptability and usability of the device.

Who can participate?
Children aged 4-18 years who have been referred to the Children's Epilepsy Surgery Service for inpatient video telemetry

What does the study involve?
In-hospital consented participants will have four Clic EEG devices applied in addition to their routine hospital video EEG monitoring. The devices will be applied for 3-5 days during the hospital stay. Five parents/carers will be asked to complete questionnaires on what they think of the device and whether or not it appears easy to use. The study aims to find out how Clic EEG compares to video EEG data with regard to being able to diagnose epileptic seizures. 

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Mild risks associated with medical tape (to which the devices are attached) causing soreness or irritation. There are no recorded side effects in healthy volunteers. There will be no direct benefit to participants as the devices will not be used diagnostically but this first-in-child study will go toward establishing the effectiveness and safety of the device.

Where is the study run from?
Bristol Children's Hospital (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expecting to run for?
June 2026 to March 2027

Who is funding the study?
This study is funded by an NIHR i4i grant (UK)

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Children aged 4-18 years
2. Referred to the Children's Epilepsy Surgery Service (CESS) at University Hospitals Bristol & Weston for inpatient vEEG monitoring
3. For the qualitative interviews: parents/carers of enrolled children and clinical staff (neurologists, neurophysiologists, nurses) involved in their care
Exclusion criteria:
1. Evidence of significant scalp swelling or injury (e.g., cuts, infections)
2. Known skin allergies to medical adhesives
3. Co-enrolment in another clinical study if their clinical team believes that this could impact the study results or cause undue burden
4. If the clinical care team deems it inappropriate for them to be approached about the study
